steps.title: A pawn down
steps.source: The following position is an excellent proof of the value of the opposition as a means of defence. White is a Pawn behind and apparently lost, yet he can manage to draw.

narration.say: White is a pawn behind, and apparently lost. Yet he can draw, with the opposition.
But not the close opposition: the pawns do not allow it. White takes the distant opposition.

feedback.Kf1: Close opposition: Kd2, Kf2, Kd3, and your own pawn on f3 stops you keeping the lateral opposition.
feedback.*: The king goes to the corner, on the same rank as the black king.

exercise.prompt: White to move. Take the distant opposition.

narration.say: King to h2, king to d3. King to h3!
Black goes to e2, White to g2. King to e3, king to g3.
Black tries d4, and the king attacks the pawn: g4.
Black must return to e3, and White goes back to g3. He always keeps the opposition.
Back to the start. King to h1, and Black pushes g4.
White must not take: after fxg4, e4 wins.

feedback.fxg4: Then e4, and the black pawn cannot be stopped.
feedback.*: Bring the king back towards the centre.

exercise.prompt: White to move. Do not take.

narration.say: Now White takes, and Black pushes e4.
Mere counting shows that both sides queen: a draw.
In nearly all king and pawn endings, the opposition is of paramount importance.
